correctness.rationale: For \(0<\varepsilon<\var\(\varepsilon_0\)\) the fixed-cost domain maps bijectively to the 5-simplex of dose fractions. The simple eigenvalue 2 of the five-cycle adjacency gives a uniform C2-in-u spectral expansion, with explicitly checked reduced-resolvent coefficient \(Q=\tfrac4{25}(E-N)\). The support-shifting proof bounds \(E\le1/4\) for every point and shows equality for Q only at five adjacent equal pairs. At each such pair, positive first-derivative gaps exclude off-edge coordinates for every sufficiently small epsilon, while strict negative edge-face second derivative and reflection force the exact equal split. Compactness exhausts all global maximizers. Exact symbolic checker independently verifies rational matrix/charpoly algebra. Proof is infinite-domain analytical, not inferred from finite tests; no explicit \(\varepsilon_0\) is claimed.

originality.rationale: The primary open-access paper treats exactly the symmetric-circle matrix but in Section 2.4 explicitly supplies only the transmission-stopping minimization theorem and numerical anti-Pareto examples for twelve nodes, not the analytical five-node small-budget maximum or its uniqueness. The related 2022 disconnected-population theorem, 2024 sufficient convexity/concavity criteria, and 2018 inverse-M-matrix minimization results do not imply the claim under their stated hypotheses. Targeted published-result and literature searches produced no precise or logically dominating coverage. Residual risks remain and no independent priority check is asserted.

value.rationale: The original literature states symmetric-circle optimization is analytically unresolved for \(N\ge5\) beyond the zero-transmission cost, and offers only numerical 12-group anti-Pareto trajectories. The first such case, the five-node odd cycle, has a meaningful exact small-budget worst-allocation question. The theorem identifies every optimizer for an entire positive cost interval and a nonzero second-order cost penalty for one-group concentration. The edge-versus-nonedge quadratic reveals a reusable contact-network mechanism, not a routine restatement of the Perron eigenvalue formula or an arbitrary parameter sample.
